claims.text: High configurational entropy promotes atomic-scale chemical disorder in high-entropy nanoalloys.
Chemical disorder kinetically suppresses atomic diffusion at elevated temperatures.
Suppressed atomic diffusion inhibits phase segregation at elevated temperatures.
Suppression of diffusion and phase segregation maintains structural and chemical stability.
The initial nanoalloy is single-phase, chemically disordered, and has nanoscale grains at ambient conditions.
The nanoalloy and lower-configurational-entropy comparison alloy will be annealed above 800°C under identical thermal profiles in an inert atmosphere.
High configurational entropy produces the proposed atomic-scale chemical-disorder mediator.
Chemical disorder minimizes local concentration gradients.
Minimized local concentration gradients reduce atomic mobility.
Reduced atomic mobility delays diffusion-driven phase segregation.
Reduced atomic mobility delays grain coarsening at high temperatures.
After annealing, the high-entropy nanoalloy will exhibit less grain growth than the lower-entropy control.
After annealing, the high-entropy nanoalloy will exhibit less phase segregation than the lower-entropy control.
After annealing, the high-entropy nanoalloy will retain a more uniform microstructure than the lower-entropy control.
Diffusion is significant in the stated application regime, typically above 800°C.
Five or more principal elements ensure sufficient configurational entropy for the prediction.
Surface-energy effects and segregation at nanoparticle interfaces may also influence stability.
Equal or greater phase segregation and grain growth in the high-entropy nanoalloy relative to the control would falsify the proposed suppression mechanism.
